newsitem.title: FRANCE: Communists set conditions for cabinet entry.
newsitem.headline: Communists set conditions for cabinet entry.

text.p: French Communist leader Robert Hue, highlighting differences in the left-wing opposition two days before a crucial parliamentary election runoff, spelled out on Friday his party's terms for joining a Socialist-led government.

The conditions included demands for pay rises and new taxes on investment earnings, anathema to the ruling centre-right coalition which has increasingly angled its campaign against the "perils of a Communist return to power".
Some analysts said Hue's demands, by their militant nature, could be a ploy to suggest the Communists were unlikely to be part of a left-wing cabinet.
Their absence could be a strong incentive to hesitant voters to cast ballots for a more reassuring-looking left, which sounds increasingly confident of victory in Sunday's second round.

The centre-right, easily outpolled by the combined left on last Sunday's first round, pinned its final hopes on socially minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin, hastily anointed as its new campaign leader after Prime Minister Alain Juppe's decision to resign following the poll debacle.

Seguin made a rousing speech by video-link to a conservative rally in Paris on Thursday night, but gave no indication of what his policies would be, concentrating on attacking the Socalists' record in government in the 1980s and early 1990s.
The Communists are very much a junior partner in the left-wing alliance, which also includes ecologists and radicals.
Speaking on television on Friday, Hue said: "It is impossible to imagine a Left that would not quickly launch a series of (left-wing) measures..."

Alain Bocquet, Communist floor leader in the outgoing National Assembly, said on Thursday his party would be loyal "whether we participate in a government or whether we support it without participating". He said a decision would be made at a party meeting on Monday.
The two campaign allies have bickered before over European monetary union, which the Communists oppose but the Socialists generally favour.
But Hue campaigned alongside Socialist leader Lionel Jospin in the Paris suburbs on Friday, showing their desire to win overrode tactical differences.
The Communist threat did not prevent joyous Socialists from debating draft lists of cabinet officers and weighing legislative strategy should they take power.
An elated Jospin said late on Thursday that a leftist win would stun but also cheer Europe as it would follow Labour's victory in Britain.

"We are on the brink of an event that is going to astound Europe, but it will also raise a magnificent hope in Europe after the victory of the leftist Labour Party in Great Britain," Jospin told a rally in the northern city of Lille.
"This evening, I am telling you, we can win on Sunday," Jospin told a cheering crowd of backers.

Conservative President Jacques Chirac called the election 10 months early to seek a new five-year lease for his centre-right government and a "new elan" for France as it prepared to join a single European currency.
But Chirac badly misjudged voters' dismay at record 12.8 percent unemployment and government austerity programmes adopted to help France qualify for the euro common currency.

The left scored an upset win over the governing centre-right in last Sunday's first-round vote, forcing Chirac to contemplate the prospect of a leftist majority sharing power with him in an arrangement known in France as "cohabitation".
The humiliating upset forced the unpopular Juppe to take the blame and announce he would step down after Sunday's vote.
